one_liner: Python generator emitting lazily-reduced Plantard NTTs (C/Jasmin) for ML-KEM/ML-DSA/FN-DSA; 1.5-2.5x faster than pq-crystals reference NTT.
what_it_does: This is a research artifact, not a library. A Python/Jinja2 generator (lazygenerator.py) takes a parameter triple (q, n, omega) and emits specialized forward and inverse NTT code in portable C or Jasmin. The artifact also ships patched copies of the pq-crystals Kyber and Dilithium reference trees that use that code. The only formally verified output is the Jasmin ML-KEM NTT, which is proved equivalent to the formosa-mlkem specification in EasyCrypt; the C output is unverified. What you get is ntt()/invntt() working in place on an int16_t/int32_t[n] array, and adopting it also means moving the scheme's internal Montgomery domain to Plantard (tomont constant, basemul, pointwise multiply).
how_it_is_fast: It uses Plantard multiplication by a precomputed twiddle (Huang et al.). This needs one fewer multiplication per butterfly than Montgomery and leaves outputs in a tighter centered range, so fewer Barrett/Montgomery reduction passes are needed. At generation time, a static bound analyzer tracks per-layer coefficient growth: the CT butterfly grows additively and the GS plus-arm doubles. It inserts a reduction only on layers where the signed word would otherwise overflow. Per the paper, ML-KEM needs one reduction (inverse layer 3), ML-DSA none and FN-DSA-1024 several. Each layer is emitted as its own loop with len and k baked in as constants, so there is no runtime branch on the layer index.
when_to_use: Scalar or portable ML-KEM/ML-DSA builds derived from the pq-crystals reference C, such as generic x86-64 packages that cannot assume AVX2 or other 64-bit targets, where the NTT is a measurable share of decapsulation or signing.
ML-DSA scalar code: the generated NTT beat mldsa-native's scalar C (OPT=0 AUTO=0) by 1.66x forward and 1.52x inverse in the paper's Table 2.
Generating an NTT for a new NTT-friendly modulus (q prime, n a power of two, n | q-1; complete or incomplete NTT) without hand-tuning where reductions go.
Verification or research work that needs a Plantard-based ML-KEM NTT with an EasyCrypt proof chain down to the formosa-mlkem spec (Jasmin backend, x86-64).
when_not_to_use: AVX2, AVX-512 or NEON-optimized ML-KEM/ML-DSA deployments: there is no vector backend. The authors measured their hand-tuned Plantard AVX2 about 10% (16-bit, ML-KEM) and 28% (32-bit, ML-DSA) slower than Montgomery AVX2.

When mlkem-native scalar C is the baseline: under gcc -O3 the generated ML-KEM forward NTT is slower (0.86x) because its 32-bit intermediate halves auto-vectorization lanes. Only the inverse wins (1.18x).
When you need a maintained, packaged library: the code exists only as an ephemeral double-blind anonymous.4open.science mirror with no releases, issue tracker or public git history.
When you need verified C: the C backend, the ML-DSA/FN-DSA outputs and the Python generator are all unverified. The paper also notes that constant-time behavior of the C depends on the compiler.
When you expect big whole-scheme wins: end-to-end gains are only 1.08x-1.32x because the NTT is a small share of total cycles (3,876 cycles of the roughly 91k-122k per ML-KEM-512 operation).

integration.dependencies: Generated C: none beyond <stdint.h> (__int128 when q >= 2^32). Generator: Python >= 3.9 with click, jinja2 and pycryptodome. Jasmin path: the Jasmin compiler. Proofs: EasyCrypt with the Jasmin library and an SMT solver.
integration.min_toolchain: Generator needs Python 3.9+. The C output was tested only with gcc 11.4 (-O3 -fomit-frame-pointer), and the L=64 path needs GCC/Clang __int128. The Jasmin output was built with Jasmin 2025.6.1 and clang-14.
integration.platforms: Generated C is portable scalar code but was benchmarked only on x86-64 (Intel Xeon E-2314). Jasmin output is x86-64 only. No SIMD paths.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The generated ntt()/invntt() read only const twiddle tables and transform the caller's array in place; the files read have no global mutable state.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — Kyber keeps pq-crystals' ntt()/invntt() signatures, and in Dilithium invntt_tomont() becomes invntt(). Integration also replaces reduce.c/h and edits poly.c: the tomont constant, invntt_tomont now calls poly_tomont first, poly_reduce after ntt is removed, and basemul/pointwise use Plantard. The paper reports NIST KAT outputs bit-identical to the reference.

gotchas: The scalar plantard_reduce() added to reduce.c multiplies signed values that overflow (int32 x PLAN_QINV for Kyber, int64 x PLAN_QINV for Dilithium). That is undefined behavior in C, and the Makefiles do not pass -fwrapv. The generated plantard_mul_reduce in ntt.c avoids this with unsigned casts.

The README says the generator also produces the EasyCrypt proofs, but it only renders code templates. The paper lists proof emission as future work, and only the q=3329 ML-KEM Jasmin instance is proved.

analyzer.py computes the Plantard input range (plan_bnd), but its per-layer reduction decisions check only the signed storage bound. Outputs for new parameter sets should be tested, not assumed correct.

The shipped harnesses are asymmetric. The baseline kyber/dilithium test_speed.c keeps NTESTS 1000 and has no NTT+INVNTT row, while the Plantard variants use 10000. The paper states 10k iterations for all runs.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Dilithium-AVX512 (ML-DSA) and VecFalcon (Falcon signing) are vector-ISA implementations and win only where AVX-512/AVX2/NEON etc. are available. Pick this for scalar/portable ML-KEM or ML-DSA built on the pq-crystals reference, or when you need a verified ML-KEM NTT; no sibling covers ML-KEM (fasthqc is HQC).
verified_claims_summary: On an Intel Xeon E-2314 with turbo and HT off, using gcc 11.4 -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer, the generated NTT was dropped into the pq-crystals reference C. It cut forward/inverse NTT cycles by 1.83x/2.48x for ML-KEM, 1.73x/1.78x for ML-DSA and 1.47x/1.66x for FN-DSA-1024. End to end that gives 1.08x-1.32x (ML-KEM-512 decaps 162,047 to 122,499 cycles; ML-DSA-2 sign 1.26x). It is 1.26x/2.19x vs the formosa-mlkem Jasmin NTT and 0.86x/1.18x vs mlkem-native scalar C, and the artifact's kyber.csv/dilithium.csv/falcon1024.csv medians match the paper's tables.
